newsitem.title: INDIA: India PM sees better foreign ties, economic growth.
newsitem.headline: India PM sees better foreign ties, economic growth.

text.p: India's new centre-left Prime Minister, Inder Kumar Gujral, said on Saturday that he aimed to boost ties with arch-rival Pakistan and put the economy on a high-growth path.

Gujral, 77, who was sworn in on Monday after a leadership change in the 15-party United Front, told Reuters Television in an interview he looked forward to a summit meeting with Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif in May.
"When I look at the past few weeks gone by, I think India-Pakistan relationships have improved a great deal," said Gujral, who was foreign minister prior to becoming prime minister.
He was referring to official talks which resumed in March after a three-year-gap, marking a thaw between the two neighbours who have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947.
Gujral met Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan earlier this month.
"Now, as prime minister, when I meet Mr. Nawaz Sharif...I will resume links, and I think we are moving towards discovering more and more areas of cooperation," Gujral said.

Gujral became prime minister for the United Front under a politial deal with a vital ally, the Congress party. The Congress on April 11 overturned the 10-month rule of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, whose removal it had sought.

Gujral and Sharif, who won power in elections earlier this year, are expected to meet next month in the Maldivian capital of Male on the fringes of a summit of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).

Official talks between India and Pakistan in 1994 had broken down over Kashmir, the disputed region over which the two neighbours have fought two wars. New Delhi rules two-thirds and Islamabad a third of the Himalayan region.
Coinciding with the resumption of talks, India eased visa restrictions for visitors from Pakistan, which in turn freed Indian fishermen caught in its territorial waters.
The two nations are also inching towards freer trade, and this week signed an agreement on narcotics control.

Gujral said the Indian economy, which launched an economic reforms programme in 1991, could start on a high economic growth path even if his coalition could meet just 10 percent of its objectives laid out in a common minimum programme (CMP).

"India is on the march. I have no doubt (about) that," Gujral said, and referred to India's 7.0 percent growth in 1996/97 (April-March). "If we are able to touch what the CMP has spelt, even 10 percent, we have taken off. That is my objective."
The common programme envisages foreign investment in the order of $10 billion every year, compared with less than $2.0 billion in 1995/96.
Gujral said India looked forward to investment in areas like infrastructure, but that did not mean a bar on others.
To a question on relations with the United States, Gujral said he aimed for stronger ties based on mutual respect.
New Delhi and Washington, which saw India as too close to the former Soviet Union, have edged closer since 1991, when India launched its economic reforms.
